name: Polyquaternium-10

lead: Polyquaternium-10 is a modified cellulose polymer used in shampoos and conditioners to leave hair easier to comb, softer and smoother-looking, with less frizz and a creamier lather.

Its positive charge draws it to negatively charged hair, where it deposits as a thin conditioning film that reduces friction between strands. Formulation literature credits cationic polymers like it with easier combing and smoother hair; it has also been studied in hydrogels and sensors, but not as a stand-alone hair treatment.

paras: People use it by choosing shampoos or conditioners that list it. It is a background ingredient, working alongside other conditioning agents in the formula, and the smoother feel is noticeable after each wash.
No specific safety findings for hair or skin were reported in the sources reviewed. As with any cosmetic ingredient, individual sensitivities are possible.

angle.text: Polyquaternium-10 is a polymer that coats the hair shaft in shampoos and conditioners, cutting friction and frizz so hair combs easily and looks smoother and shinier after washing. It works as part of the product formula rather than as a separate treatment.

lead: Polyquaternium-10 (PQ-10) is the INCI name for quaternized hydroxyethyl cellulose, a cellulose-derived polymer carrying positively charged quaternary ammonium groups.[1] It belongs to the polyquaternium family, of which at least 40 members have been approved under the cosmetic naming system.[1]

It is used in shampoos and conditioners to make hair look and feel smoother. Positively charged polymers bind to hair, which carries a net negative charge when damaged, and are described as providing conditioning, smoothing, easier combing and creamier lather.[2][3] The chain is simple: the polymer deposits on the hair fibre, smooths the surface and reduces static, and the hair detangles more easily and looks neater and shinier.[3]

It is a background ingredient rather than a product people seek out by name, though it appears on ingredient lists of many hair products. Outside cosmetics it has been studied in hydrogels, drug-delivery matrices, ophthalmic formulations and sensors.[4][5][6]
infobox: Positive charge binds to hair and skin[1]

paras: Polyquaterniums are polymers with many positively charged quaternary ammonium groups. The number after the name reflects registration order rather than chemical similarity, so neighbouring numbers can be very different structures; PQ-6 is a diallyldimethylammonium homopolymer, PQ-10 is quaternized hydroxyethyl cellulose, PQ-11 a vinylpyrrolidone copolymer and PQ-29 a modified chitosan.[1]

Research papers describe PQ-10 as a chloro-2-hydroxy-3-(trimethylamino)propyl polyethylene glycol cellulose and have studied commercial grades of different molecular mass.[7][8] Its interactions with surfactants such as sodium dodecyl sulfate, common in shampoos, have been examined in the laboratory.[9]

A 2000 review of conditioning polymers in shampoos described cationic polymers as important for conditioning and smoothing, and noted the move from 2-in-1 to 3-in-1 shampoos.[2] Their positive charge lets them bind to hair and skin and helps neutralise the negative charge on hair proteins and in shampoos.[1]

Wikipedia's article on hair conditioner explains that conditioners work by coating strands rather than repairing keratin; damaged hair carries a net negative charge, and cationic polymers such as PQ-10 help reduce static and form a light film, working alongside cationic surfactants and silicones.[3] It lists detangling, shine and static control as the main effects, and notes that some other advertised benefits are marketed more than demonstrated.[3]
Polyquaterniums are also used in hair mousses, sprays, dyes, personal lubricants and contact lens solutions.[1]

PQ-10 has been cross-linked into hydrogels characterised as pH- and ion-sensitive drug-delivery systems,[4] studied with surfactants and thickeners,[10] and used in an ionic hydrogel for flexible thermal sensors.[5] It has also been tested in ophthalmic formulations: a 2015 study reported that PQ-10 gel showed no significant cytotoxicity difference from an HPMC control in two cell lines and no significant inflammation difference in rabbits.[11] Additional papers explore antibacterial nanocomposites and 3D-printed tablet matrices.[12][13] These are not appearance applications.

Reference articles on the family do not discuss toxicity or regulatory status beyond naming.[1] A 2013 study examined IgE against quaternary ammonium ions in hairdressers and bakers, groups professionally exposed to quaternary ammonium compounds, in relation to reactions to neuromuscular blocking agents in anaesthesia; it concerned the wider compound class rather than PQ-10 specifically.[14] A 2022 study reported on adsorption of PQ-10 grades to activated sludge solids as a model of removal from domestic sewage.[15]

sections.h: How it affects the look of hair
paras: For appearance, polyquaternium-10 works on the surface of the hair fibre. Shampoo leaves hair rougher and more negatively charged, and the positively charged polymer is drawn to those sites, where it forms a thin film that smooths the cuticle, reduces static and lets strands slide past each other.[3][2] The visible results people look for are hair that detangles with less pulling, feels softer, looks shinier and has fewer flyaways, and a shampoo that produces a creamier lather.[2]

Wikipedia's conditioner article adds that conditioners coat the fibre and fill in cuticle damage rather than biologically repairing it, since the hair shaft is dead tissue; damaged, bleached or heat-styled hair carries more negative charge and so tends to attract more conditioning polymer.[3] That is the logic behind including cationic polymers in products aimed at colour-treated or frequently styled hair.

PQ-10 is one of several conditioning agents that formulators combine in a shampoo or conditioner. Hair-conditioner formulas typically pair cationic polymers with cationic surfactants, silicones, fatty alcohols, humectants and acidifiers, each contributing a different effect such as slip, shine or moisture retention.[3] The 2000 review of conditioning polymers noted the industry's move from 2-in-1 to 3-in-1 shampoos, where polymer deposition has to survive the rinsing of a detergent system.[2] Rheology work has also examined how cationic celluloses interact with surfactants and thickeners, a factor in how the finished product pours and feels.[10]

Because it is a background ingredient, consumers rarely choose PQ-10 by name. It appears on the ingredient lists of shampoos, conditioners, mousses and styling sprays and is read as a sign that a product is built to condition.[1]

The numbers in the polyquaternium naming scheme reflect the order in which ingredients were registered, not chemical similarity. PQ-6 is a diallyldimethylammonium homopolymer, PQ-10 is a cellulose derivative, PQ-11 is a vinylpyrrolidone copolymer and PQ-29 is a modified chitosan.[1] Statements about one member of the family therefore do not automatically apply to another, and readers comparing ingredient lists are looking at structurally different materials.
No studies found. A registered phase 2 trial of probiotic-containing hair products (NCT04566549, 21 participants) is not a study of PQ-10.[16]

timeline.event: A review of conditioning polymers in shampoo formulations describes the role of cationic polymers and the shift toward 3-in-1 shampoos. [2]
Research describes cross-linked cationic cellulose hydrogels, an early materials application of the polymer family. [4]
A study reports the ocular biocompatibility of a polyquaternium-10 gel in cell lines and rabbits. [11]
